steps: Learn the key vocabulary for family members
Master adjective agreement rules for gender and number
Use ser for personality traits and tener for physical features
Build extended descriptions using connectives like pero, también and además
method_card.title: Family and Describing People
method_card.content:
This lesson covers family members, physical appearance and personality adjectives. Two key grammar rules underpin everything: use ser for personality and permanent characteristics, and tener for physical features like hair and eyes.

SpanishEnglish
la madre / el padremother / father
el hermano / la hermanabrother / sister
el abuelo / la abuelagrandfather / grandmother
el primo / la primacousin (m/f)
el padrastro / la madrastrastepfather / stepmother
el hijo / la hijason / daughter
alto/atall
bajo/ashort
delgado/aslim
mayor / menorolder / younger
simpático/anice, friendly
gracioso/afunny
trabajador(a)hardworking
perezoso/alazy
amablekind (Higher)

Grammar focus: ser vs tener for descriptions. Use ser for personality and permanent traits: Es simpática (She is nice). Use tener for hair and eyes: Tiene el pelo largo (She has long hair). Never say está simpática for personality — estar is for temporary states and locations.

Adjectives ending in -o change to -a for feminine, -os/-as for plural. Adjectives ending in -e (e.g. inteligente) only add -s for plural. Mayor and menor never change for gender.

Model paragraph: Mi madre es alta y delgada con el pelo largo y moreno. Es muy simpática y trabajadora. Me llevo muy bien con ella. (My mother is tall and slim with long dark hair. She is very nice and hardworking. I get on very well with her.)

exam_context.frequency: Core topic — family descriptions appear across speaking, listening, reading and writing every year

gold.source_text: In my family there are five people. I live with my mother, my stepfather and my two brothers. My older brother is very funny but sometimes lazy.
model_answers: En mi familia somos cinco personas. Vivo con mi madre, mi padrastro y mis dos hermanos. Mi hermano mayor es muy gracioso pero a veces perezoso.

steps: Learn the key vocabulary for friendships and qualities
Master the reflexive verb llevarse bien/mal con
Use ser for personality traits — never estar
Practice opinion phrases like Creo que and A mi modo de ver
method_card.title: Friendships and Personal Qualities
method_card.content:
This lesson covers friendship vocabulary, the qualities you value in a friend, and how to spend time together. Key grammar: the reflexive verb llevarse bien/mal con (to get on well/badly with) and a range of opinion phrases beyond me gusta.

SpanishEnglish
el/la mejor amigo/abest friend
la amistadfriendship
la confianzatrust
el apoyosupport
el respetorespect
fielloyal
comprensivo/aunderstanding
honesto/ahonest
divertido/afun
generoso/agenerous
llevarse bien conto get on well with
llevarse mal conto get on badly with
Creo que / Pienso queI think that
A mi modo de verIn my view (Higher)
desde hace + timefor + time period (Higher)

Grammar focus: reflexive verbs and ser for personality. Llevarse is a reflexive verb: me llevo, te llevas, se lleva, nos llevamos, os lleváis, se llevan. Follow it with con + the person. Use ser for personality: es fiel (she is loyal), es honesto (he is honest). Do NOT use estar for permanent personality traits — está honesto is wrong.

Opinion phrases: Creo que, Pienso que, En mi opinión, A mi modo de ver. These all take a clause directly: Creo que la confianza es lo más importante (I think trust is the most important thing).

Model paragraph: Me llevo muy bien con mi mejor amiga porque es fiel y comprensiva. Creo que la confianza es lo más importante en una amistad. (I get on very well with my best friend because she is loyal and understanding. I think trust is the most important thing in a friendship.)

exam_context.frequency: Core topic — friendship and qualities appear across all papers

gold.source_text: In my view, the most important thing in a friendship is trust. A good friend should be loyal, honest and understanding. Sometimes we argue but we always forgive each other quickly.
model_answers: A mi modo de ver, lo más importante en una amistad es la confianza. Un buen amigo debe ser fiel, honesto y comprensivo. A veces discutimos pero siempre nos perdonamos rápidamente.

Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences about grammar accuracy","improvement":"optional specific correction"}

misconceptions.message: You picked this because 'llevamos mal' and 'nada' look similar to the words here, but the sentence actually says bien and mucho, meaning they get on well, not badly.
You picked this because 'nos' can look like it refers to one person, but 'nos llevamos' always means 'we get on', not 'I get on with him'.
You picked this because 'común' looks like 'common' as in famous, but here it means shared interests, so 'we get on' not 'they are common'.

You picked this because it's a common opinion-sounding phrase, but 'me gusta mucho' means 'I like it a lot', not 'in my view'.

method_card.title: Relationships and Future Plans
method_card.content:
This lesson covers relationships, marriage and family life, and how to talk about future plans using the near future (ir a + infinitive) and the conditional (I would). These are among the most tested structures in writing and speaking assessments.

SpanishEnglish
la parejacouple / partner

Grammar focus: near future and conditional. Near future: voy a + infinitive (e.g. Voy a casarme = I am going to get married). Conditional: add -ía endings to the infinitive (e.g. casaría, viviría, tendría). Irregular conditional stems: tendr-, podr-, querr-, har-. Me gustaría = I would like — always followed by the infinitive: Me gustaría tener dos hijos.

Note: estar casado/a uses estar because being married is a state, not a permanent identity. Contrast with ser soltero/a, which can use either depending on context.

Model paragraph: En el futuro, me gustaría casarme y tener dos hijos. Mi boda ideal sería en la playa con toda mi familia. (In the future, I would like to get married and have two children. My ideal wedding would be on the beach with all my family.)

method_card.title: Equality and Inclusion
method_card.content:
This lesson covers equality, fairness and discrimination — a Higher-tier topic requiring abstract opinion language. You need to express views confidently, use connectives like sin embargo and aunque, and deploy the present subjunctive after impersonal expressions.

SpanishEnglish
la igualdadequality
la desigualdadinequality
la discriminacióndiscrimination
el racismoracism
el sexismosexism
la justiciajustice, fairness
los derechosrights
defenderto defend
comprometerseto commit / to engage
el compromisocommitment
respetarto respect
tratar a alguien con respetoto treat someone with respect
hay que + infinitiveone must / it is necessary to
sin embargohowever
aunquealthough / even though

Grammar focus: the present subjunctive after impersonal expressions. At Higher tier, you must use the subjunctive after expressions like es importante que, es necesario que, es fundamental que. The present subjunctive is formed by taking the yo present form, dropping the -o, and adding the opposite endings: -ar verbs take -e endings; -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.

Examples: Es importante que respetemos a todos. (It is important that we respect everyone.) Es necesario que haya igualdad. (It is necessary that there be equality.)

Opinion verbs: Creo que, Opino que, Pienso que, A mi modo de ver, En mi opinión. Connectives: sin embargo, aunque, por otro lado, a pesar de que, no obstante.

Model paragraph: Creo que la discriminación es un problema grave. Es importante que todos luchemos por la igualdad, aunque todavía hay mucho trabajo por hacer. Sin embargo, opino que la situación está mejorando poco a poco. (I think discrimination is a serious problem. It is important that we all fight for equality, although there is still a lot of work to do. However, I think the situation is gradually improving.)

exam_context.frequency: Higher-tier topic — abstract opinion language and subjunctive are rewarded in writing and speaking

Check: subjunctive after es importante que, aunque + indicative/subjunctive, comprometerse, hay que. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences about grammar accuracy","improvement":"optional specific correction"}

gaps.rule: Present subjunctive of luchar after es fundamental que

gaps.rule: Present subjunctive of ser after aunque

wrong.es: es is indicative (it is — as a fact). After aunque expressing a hypothetical, use the subjunctive → sea.
wrong.est\u00e1: está is estar (not ser). For abstract qualities like 'difficult' use ser (subjunctive: sea).

gaps.correct_explain: sea is the present subjunctive of ser, used after aunque when the meaning is 'even though it might be'. Aunque + subjunctive = even if (uncertain); aunque + indicative = although (fact).

You picked this because 'igualdad' and 'desigualdad' look similar when skimming fast, but the sentence clearly says igualdad, meaning equality, not inequality.

options: En mi opinión, la discriminación es inaceptable.
En mi opinión, la discriminación está inaceptable.

misconceptions.message: You picked this because 'está' feels like a normal way to say 'is', but permanent qualities and opinions use ser, so 'es inaceptable' is correct, not 'está'.
You picked this because translating word-for-word from English puts 'es' straight after opinión, but Spanish needs the verb after the subject, giving 'la discriminación es'.
You picked this because 'ser' looks like the basic verb 'to be', but you must conjugate it to match the subject, giving 'es' rather than the infinitive.

method_card.title: Identity and Self-Description
method_card.content:
This lesson covers who you are: your nationality, the languages you speak, your values and how you introduce yourself. The central grammar point is ser + adjective for identity, with careful attention to lowercase nationalities and adjective agreement.

SpanishEnglish
soy inglés / soy inglesaI am English (m/f)
español / españolaSpanish (m/f)
francés / francesaFrench (m/f)
alemán / alemanaGerman (m/f)
galés / galesaWelsh (m/f)
irlandés / irlandesaIrish (m/f)
hablo español / inglés / francésI speak Spanish / English / French
soy bilingüeI am bilingual
los valoresvalues
la identidadidentity
me llamomy name is
tengo … añosI am … years old
provengo deI come from (Higher)
las raícesroots / origins (Higher)

Grammar focus: nationalities are NOT capitalised in Spanish. This is a critical Spanish-specific rule. Write soy inglés, NOT soy Inglés. Write hablo español, NOT hablo Español. Only the country name takes a capital: España, Francia, Alemania, Gales.

Nationality adjectives agree for gender: inglés (m) / inglesa (f). Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a for feminine. Use ser for nationality (permanent identity): Soy inglés. Never estoy inglés.

Model paragraph: Me llamo Pablo, tengo dieciséis años y soy inglés. Mis padres son de España, así que hablo español e inglés. En mi opinión, ser bilingüe es una ventaja enorme. (My name is Pablo, I am sixteen and I am English. My parents are from Spain, so I speak Spanish and English. In my opinion, being bilingual is a huge advantage.)

gaps.rule: Adjective agreement — te refers to the speaker

wrong.ricas: ricas is feminine plural. The subject is a single person → rico or rica.
wrong.ricos: ricos is plural. The subject is a single person → rico (masculine) or rica (feminine).

gaps.correct_explain: rico agrees with a masculine speaker (or rica for feminine). The adjective describes te (you), so it agrees with the person speaking.

wrong.es: es is the present indicative. After aunque for a concession expressing uncertainty, the subjunctive is preferred at Higher tier.
wrong.puede ser: puede ser (indicative) after aunque treats the difficulty as a stated fact. Using the subjunctive (pueda ser) is preferred in Higher tier writing to indicate that you are acknowledging a possibility rather than a certainty.

gaps.correct_explain: pueda ser uses the subjunctive of poder (pueda) because aunque + subjunctive signals a hypothetical or concessive meaning ('even if it might be'). Alternatively sea (subjunctive of ser) also works.

options: Me llamo Lucía, tengo quince años y soy irlandesa.

bronze.question: Which sentence correctly says 'My name is Lucía, I am fifteen and I am Irish'?

misconceptions.message: You capitalised Irlandesa because English capitalises nationalities. Spanish doesn't do this — nationality adjectives like irlandesa stay lowercase, even though the country name España is capitalised.
You used estoy for age because estar covers many 'states' in English thinking. But age uses tener (tengo quince años) — Spanish treats age as something you 'have', not something you 'are'.
You used estoy for nationality, treating it like a temporary state. Nationality is a permanent characteristic, so it needs ser: soy irlandesa, not estoy irlandesa.

options: I speak English, French and a bit of Spanish
I speak English, French and a lot of Spanish
I spoke English, French and a bit of Spanish

bronze.question: What does 'Hablo inglés, francés y un poco de español' mean?

misconceptions.message: You read un poco as 'a lot' because mucho and poco can blur together when translating quickly. Un poco de means 'a little/a bit of', so it's the opposite — a small amount of Spanish.
You translated hablo as 'spoke' perhaps from spotting a similar-looking form. Hablo is present tense (I speak) — the past 'I spoke' would need hablé, a different ending.
